title: Levi Yitzchak, the people's lawyer
hookLine: Levi Yitzchak's commentary finds merit in the people in every portion
tomorrow: a prayer that asks to see people's virtues, not their faults?

lines: MAYBE SHE DIDN'T SEE THE MESSAGE.
cards: Every group chat has the friend nobody appointed: the one who says, wait, maybe she didn't see the message. Every single time.
Hasidic stories have a friend like that at the level of heaven: Rabbi Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev, remembered as the defender of Israel, who argued the people's case before God.
One story people tell: he sees a man greasing the wheels of his wagon while still wrapped in his tallit and tefillin, mid-prayer. Anyone else might scold him.
Levi Yitzchak looks up and says: Master of the world, look at Your people. Even while they grease their wheels, they pray to You.

teach.b: Under the story sits one question: when someone falls short, which way do you lean?
Jewish teaching has an old answer in Pirkei Avot, the Ethics of the Fathers: judge every person l'chaf zechut, toward the scale's pan of merit. Levi Yitzchak lived that out loud.

His commentary on the weekly Torah portions, the Kedushat Levi, is remembered for finding merit in the people, portion after portion, and in the stories he takes their side even with God. Always the merit.
Now a neighbor tradition, in its own words.

In Paul's first letter to the Corinthians, a chapter on love says, in the King James Version, that charity, meaning love, "thinketh no evil," and "Beareth all things, believeth all things, hopeth all things."
Two old traditions, side by side: before you settle on the worst, look for the good reading of a person. That's real shared ground. And the honest difference.
Paul calls it love, and ends the chapter, "the greatest of these is charity." The Mishnah's word is judgment, a fair scale, tipped kindly.
And Levi Yitzchak often turns the merit upward, as a plea: he stands before God as the people's lawyer.
One describes how love sees a neighbor; the other also argues the neighbor's case in heaven. Neither is a copy of the other. Both lean the same way.

how: Jews learn the teaching to judge others favorably, dan l'chaf zechut, from Pirkei Avot, often studied on Shabbat afternoons; Levi Yitzchak's Kedushat Levi is studied on the weekly Torah portion, and stories of him pleading for the people are told especially around the High Holy Days.

o: leaning toward the good reading of a person, and pleading their case
points of merit that God adds up at the very end of a person's life
the merit of the ancestors, which protects their children's children

games.q: two traditions leaning the same way — tap the pairs.
p: argued the people's case before God
toward the scale's pan of merit
his commentary on the Torah portions

s: judging toward merit means pretending nothing went wrong
you see the shortfall; you lean toward the good reading of the person.
in the stories, Levi Yitzchak defends the people even before God
the man greasing his wheels at prayer: look, even now they pray to You.
Paul's chapter on love and Pirkei Avot say exactly the same thing
both lean toward the good reading; Paul calls it love, the Mishnah a fair scale, and Levi Yitzchak makes it a plea.

games.q: a classmate posts a vague, gloomy message, and people start guessing she's fishing for attention. what would Levi Yitzchak's way look like?
o: read it toward merit: check in with her, privately and kindly.
join the guessing; posts like that are usually about attention.
stay out of it; leaning either way isn't really your place.
games.why: Pirkei Avot says judge every person toward merit, and Levi Yitzchak took that all the way to heaven. the good reading comes first.

practice: Bring to mind someone who let you down this week in a small way. In your notes app, or as a real message, write them a few lines that start from the most generous reading of what happened.
You don't have to send it; for the rest of the sit, just read it back slowly and see how it sits.

wordCard.voice: Always the merit: Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev's way. Judge every person toward merit, and when it counts, argue their case.

orig.note: Hebrew: the scale's pan of merit; to judge l'chaf zechut is to lean toward the good reading of a person.

carryVoice: Your line: judge every person toward merit, the good reading before the worst one. Shalom for now.
